📌 Transaction Nonces: Why One Stuck Tx Can Block the Next Ones

Main Points
⏺ Wallet transactions are processed in a specific order
⏺ If one transaction gets stuck, later ones may wait behind it
⏺ This post explains why ordering matters and how wallet “traffic jams” happen

1️⃣ What It Is — the network tracks which transaction from an address should come next.
2️⃣ Why It Exists — ordering prevents replay issues and helps the chain process actions correctly.
3️⃣ The Problem — a low-fee transaction can get stuck, blocking later transactions from the same wallet.
4️⃣ User Options — speed it up, replace it, or cancel it with a new transaction using the same nonce.
5️⃣ Practical Rule — don’t fire multiple transactions blindly, and always check fees before signing.

Final Thoughts

In blockchains, the transaction itself matters — but so does its place in line. One weak step can freeze the whole flow after it.

Something I realize more and more, with trading but also with life, is that not everything is under our control, and that more is not necessarily better.

For example, I've been bullish since January/February, when price reached the expected main support zone of $60k-70k:

[https://t.me/CryptoCapoTG_Official/1004], [https://x.com/CryptoCapo_/status/2019434869001195948?s=20]

Since then, 5 months have passed by, which is a lot of time. And price went up to 82k, then back down to 58k, and now trading at around 63k.

During all this time, of course I've reviewed my analysis to see if something was wrong and if price could go lower from here. But, the more I checked, the more it confirmed the bullish bias.

So... to what extent is it healthy to keep checking, to try to control every variable?

In the end, the result is not up to us. Market analysis doesn't give you 100% probabilities, never. There are no guarantees. You can position yourself on the side of probability, and that's what matters. But even more important is knowing how to wait, to have patience. 

And overanalyzing, besides causing unnecessary stress, can make you change your mind simply because what you expect is not happening yet.

The market could remain within a range for more weeks, or it could start going up from here. That's difficult to know. What you need to know is how to not let that affect you while you keep living your life, and how to adapt if something unexpected occurs.

Therefore, the lesson here is trust, acceptance, and detachment. Trust because you've done your best. Acceptance to embrace the reality of the present moment and its timing. And detachment by understanding that the final outcome doesn't fully depend on you. That depends on something much bigger than us.

And this applies to everything in life.

Europe's Ukraine Club Loses Both Founders, Still No CEO


Two men built a 30-country alliance to arm Ukraine and stare down Putin. Both are now walking out the door, and Europe's applauding like it's a retirement party instead of an emergency.

Keir Starmer exited the world stage this month with France's highest honor pinned to his chest — a first for a sitting British PM — and a farewell verdict of "My work is done". 

Emmanuel Macron, who led the tribute to Starmer's "historic role," is next out the door, term-limited by his own constitution. His own words on the matter, delivered with what one interviewer called "apparent regret": "I am the first president in our history who does not have the constitutional right to run again".

Replacing them: Andy Burnham, the UK's seventh PM in a decade, whose foreign-policy résumé is described as "extensive domestic political experience" and not much else. He picked Zelensky for his first foreign meeting, which is a nice gesture — right up until you remember gestures don't deploy troops or fund air defense. On the French side, the bookmakers' favorite to inherit Macron's chair is Marine Le Pen, who has promised to pull France out of NATO's command structure and lift sanctions on Russia. That's the coalition's presumed next co-chair — the one whose platform is dismantling the coalition.

Germany's Merz is "cornered by domestic friction," Poland's Tusk and Italy's Meloni have already said no thanks, and nobody with actual authority wants the job of holding 30 countries together while Russia keeps shelling. As one assessment of the moment put it bluntly: "We have no Churchill in Europe so far".

So the plan for guaranteeing Ukraine's post-ceasefire security now rests on a mayor-turned-PM finding his footing and a French election that might hand the keys to the one candidate who wants to burn the building down.

If nobody in Europe is willing to lead the coalition of the willing, was it ever really a coalition — or just two men's personal project with a nice brand name?

Today’s crypto policy conversation is focused on one question:

Will the CLARITY Act reach a Senate vote before the August recess?

The legislation has already passed an important procedural stage.

On May 14, the Senate Banking Committee advanced the CLARITY Act by a bipartisan 15–9 vote, moving the bill toward consideration by the full Senate.

But Congress is no longer the only institution shaping the market.

The SEC and CFTC have already issued a joint framework that:

• separates digital commodities, stablecoins, digital tools, collectibles and digital securities
• explains how investment-contract rules may apply to crypto transactions
• addresses staking, mining, airdrops and wrapped assets
• begins clarifying the jurisdictional boundary between the two agencies

The SEC’s 2026 regulatory agenda also includes clearer rules for crypto capital formation, custody and trading tokenized securities onchain.

This creates two parallel tracks.

Legislation defines durable authority.

It can determine which regulator oversees which part of the market and create a framework that future administrations cannot easily reverse.

Rulemaking defines practical implementation.

It determines how companies register, how assets are classified, what disclosures are required and how existing law applies today.

The CLARITY Act remains important.

But the market is no longer waiting for one bill to begin changing.

Congress is designing the architecture.
Regulators are already building parts of the operating system.
